chunks: "Sure. I'd start with the input source, V in , and put a capacitor across it, since the buck draws pulsed current.
From the top of the input rail I draw the high-side switch, an NMOS with its drain on V in and its source on the switch node, which I'll label SW.
From SW I draw a diode to ground, with the cathode at SW and the anode on ground, so it conducts when the switch node tries to go negative.
Then from SW I draw the inductor going right to the output node. From the output node I put the output capacitor to ground and the load in parallel with it.
For the control side I add a resistor divider from V out to the feedback pin of a controller, and the controller drives the gate of the high-side FET with a PWM signal.

Then I'd say that the diode is the simplest version, and that a modern one replaces it with a low-side NFET driven complementary to the high-side, which is a synchronous buck, so it doesn't waste V f times I in the diode.
And I'd talk through the paths. When the high-side is on, current goes input, FET, inductor, load.
When it's off, the inductor current continues through the diode or low-side FET, back through the load."
